expected_evidence: Geological: a distinct Younger Dryas Boundary (YDB)-type layer at ~10,950 BCE across North American sites, with anomalous markers (nanodiamonds, platinum/iridium spikes, magnetic spherules) that could be attributed to an ionizing radiation or meltwater-forcing event
Astronomical/geological: cosmogenic nuclide anomalies (spikes in 14C, 10Be, 36Cl) in ice cores or tree rings consistent with a gamma-ray ionization pulse at the specified date

Geological: sedimentary/oceanic evidence of a meltwater pulse (e.g., a Lake Agassiz drainage event, freshwater signature in North Atlantic cores, AMOC slowdown proxies) co-occurring with the extinction horizon

Material/archaeological: North American megafaunal bone beds or kill/die-off sites clustering tightly around 10,950 BCE, and human archaeological assemblages (e.g., Clovis-related) showing disruption at the same horizon
Genetic: ancient-DNA evidence of a sharp megafaunal population bottleneck/extinction pulse dated to ~10,950 BCE, distinguishable from a more gradual Holocene decline

model-prior: existing published debate over the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis and meltwater-pulse/AMOC-collapse extinction hypotheses, which this hypothesis appears to conflate with an unusual 'gamma-ray-ionization' mechanism not commonly attached to meltwater-pulse causation in the literature I recall
response.rationale: The point-date -10950 falls essentially at the Younger Dryas onset, so I treat this as a 'younger-dryas' period case for the detectability table rather than an unspecified one. Under that table, geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) evidence classes are relatively well-preserved and heavily studied for this exact window (ice cores, varved sediments, and the YDB layer are among the most intensively sampled paleoclimate/paleoevent records in existence), so absence of a confirmed gamma-ray-ionization signature is fairly informative rather than merely a detection-gap artifact. Material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence for North American megafaunal extinction are moderately detectable and indeed well-documented, but they speak to *that an extinction occurred near this time*, not to the specific proposed mechanism (gamma-ray ionization) or to meltwater-pulse causation, which is the harder part to substantiate. A key structural issue: the hypothesis pairs actor='meltwater-pulse' with mechanism='gamma-ray-ionization' — these are not mechanistically linked in mainstream reconstructions I'm aware of (meltwater pulses are hydrological/oceanic forcing; gamma-ray ionization is an astrophysical mechanism associated with different, separate extinction hypotheses, e.g. nearby supernova or GRB proposals). This looks like a conflated or synthetically combined hypothesis, which itself is a model-prior-flagged concern rather than an evidentiary one. Given the field's high scrutiny of this exact boundary (ice cores, YDB markers, cosmogenic nuclides), if a genuine gamma-ray ionization pulse had occurred and left signatures, it plausibly would have already been reported; its absence in the record, combined with the mechanistic mismatch to the stated actor, supports the 'inconclusive' action label rather than indicating poor preservation. I set the adjustment at 0.55, slightly above the raw astronomical/geological midpoint, reflecting that this period is unusually well-instrumented for exactly this kind of anomaly search, so non-detection carries more evidentiary weight than in most other hypotheses of comparable antiquity.
